module

public import Mathlib.Analysis.InnerProductSpace.PiL2
public import Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.Orientation

@[expose] public section

scoped[EuclideanGeometry] notation "ℝ³" => EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3)

open scoped EuclideanGeometry

/-- The standard basis gives us a preferred orientation in `ℝ³`.

Note: when upstreaming this to Mathlib (and generalizing to `Fin n`) one
must be careful to avoid an instance diamond with `IsEmpty.Orientation`.
Presumably this can be avoided by assuming `[NeZero n]`. -/
noncomputable instance Module.orientedEuclideanSpaceFinThree : Module.Oriented ℝ ℝ³ (Fin 3) :=
  ⟨Basis.orientation <| PiLp.basisFun ..⟩

/-- Three dimensional euclidean space is three-dimensional. -/
instance fact_finrank_euclideanSpace_fin_three : Fact (Module.finrank ℝ ℝ³ = 3) :=
  ⟨finrank_euclideanSpace_fin⟩

findings.description: The docstring at line 30 refers to an instance named `IsEmpty.Orientation`, but no such declaration exists in the imported Mathlib. The relevant empty-index instance is `IsEmpty.oriented`. The orientation itself is mathematically correct.
findings.source_evidence: Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Orientation.lean, line 106, declares `instance (priority := 100) IsEmpty.oriented [IsEmpty ι] : Module.Oriented R M ι`. A Lean environment check confirmed that `IsEmpty.oriented` exists and `IsEmpty.Orientation` does not.

findings.description: This repeats the real, dimension-three specialization of Mathlib's existing `EuclideanSpace.instFactEqNatFinrankFin`. The distinction is instance availability: Mathlib's instance is scoped to `EuclideanSpace`, whereas this instance is global. There is no mathematical discrepancy.
findings.source_evidence: Mathlib/Analysis/InnerProductSpace/PiL2.lean, lines 210–213, already declares a scoped instance `(n : ℕ) : Fact (Module.finrank 𝕜 (EuclideanSpace 𝕜 (Fin n)) = n)`. In the scratch file, disabling the FC instance and opening `scoped EuclideanSpace` makes `#synth Fact (Module.finrank ℝ ℝ³ = 3)` return `EuclideanSpace.instFactEqNatFinrankFin 3`.
findings.suggested_fix: Reuse the existing Mathlib instance, with `open scoped EuclideanSpace` where needed. Preserve the intended instance availability if consolidating this declaration.

status_issues.recorded: @[category research open]: for every n ≥ 2, every convex subset of ℝ^(n+1) has additive VC_n dimension at most one.
status_issues.source_status: The cited counterexample by KitaKen1 already disproves this general variant at n = 2. It constructs a convex three-dimensional polyhedron with additive VC₂ dimension greater than one. The same file correctly records the specialized three-dimensional bound as disproved, but leaves this general variant tagged open.
status_issues.evidence: The cited proof at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/KitaKen1/vcdim-convex-counterexample/ad7ffff1514843c886633f5408c6456dfb2e2a49/formal-conjectures-v4.27.0/VCDimConvexCounterexample.lean proves `exists_convex_r3_not_hasAddVCNDimAtMost_two_one`. In /workspace/review/vcdim_status.lean, I checked its certificate and proved `¬ (type_of% @VCDimConvex.hasAddVCNDimAtMost_n_one_of_convex_rn_add_one)` by specializing to n = 2. The resulting theorem depends only on propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound, not sorryAx.
status_issues.suggested_change: Mark the general variant `research solved` and record its negative resolution, for example by stating the negation of the universally quantified bound and citing the same counterexample. This is a status correction, not a defect in the definition of ℝ³.

reformulations.difference: The standard orientation is represented by the positive ray of the coordinate-basis determinant alternating form, rather than directly by an equivalence class of positively oriented ordered bases.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The scratch file proves, for every basis `b : Module.Basis (Fin 3) ℝ ℝ³`, that `b.orientation = positiveOrientation ↔ 0 < Matrix.det (fun i j => b j i)`. This is exactly the standard positive-coordinate-determinant criterion. It also verifies that negating one standard basis vector gives the opposite, unequal orientation.

reformulations.difference: The largest-size statement uses `Set.ncard` over unrestricted sets, despite infinite sets having `ncard = 0`; `Set.IsIsosceles` also excludes the empty set.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: These conventions do not change the maximum-eight claim. An infinite isosceles set would contain a nine-element subset, which remains nonempty and triplewise isosceles and would contradict the stated greatest-element bound. A witness with ncard eight is necessarily finite. Excluding the empty set cannot affect a positive maximum. Thus the Lean statement expresses the source's largest possible cardinality of eight.
